title: Junos Troubleshooting: The Complete Beginner's Guide

scenes.narration: You're standing outside, and your keys are inside. You don't kick the door down. You work through it step by step.

lines.t: Locked out of your own house
Work through it step by step

scenes.heading: Finding the keys
scenes.narration: You check the last place you remember, then retrace your steps. Troubleshooting a router works exactly the same way. Check the last place you remember. Is the cable even plugged in? Retrace every step.

scenes.heading: A simple routine
scenes.narration: Here's a routine that works. Check the log. Check the link. Ping the destination. Then trace the path. Roll back as a last resort. Start with the log. Then the physical link. Ping the destination. Trace the path.

scenes.heading: Common mix-ups
scenes.narration: Three misunderstandings. A failed ping could be the source, a router, a firewall or the destination. Rebooting rarely fixes things, and logs stay on disk. And there are many logs, not just messages.

items.wrong: A failed ping means the destination is broken
items.right: It could be anything on the path

items.wrong: A reboot clears logs and fixes problems
items.right: Logs persist; it rarely fixes config

scenes.heading: Remember this
scenes.cta: Try the Courseiva Junos troubleshooting lab
scenes.narration: So, to recap. Start with the logs, then the link, then the path. A failed ping could be caused by anything along the way. And rollback is your safety net. Ready to practise? Try the Courseiva Junos troubleshooting lab.

points.t: A failed ping can have many causes
